input.add_to_description: Day 15: riding in the bait wagon to the Gannet Causeway, shackled at the feet, hands free, Pell beside him. Dry about Wren's threat to have Pell gag him.

entries.text: notebook: updated Corvin Tallowmere

You ride up beside the wagon and murmur your warning. Corvin doesn't turn his head. "Child, if I wanted to say something off the plan, I wouldn't say it aloud on the road." Pell, on his far side, says to nobody that the gag is already in his saddlebag. Corvin allows himself a small, dry smile and says nothing more for six hours.

You give the order, and the little column rolls out of the Vantry yard through the waking streets, with Kit at your elbow and the road song humming under your breath. The guards, who started stiff, ease into step. The road runs out of the town and across flat country, past reed-beds and salt-pans glittering in the sun. Nothing watches you that you can see.

A little after noon the road drops toward the flats, and the landward end of the Gannet Causeway lies before you: the tide still creeping across the gravel, the tall reeds and the drainage ditch on your side, and nine hundred paces off the drowned boat-shed on the far bank, grey against the water.

Marl Sedge rises out of the reeds a few steps from your horse so quietly that Ember doesn't even shy. Her eyes are red from the night and her voice is flat.

"Five of them, miss. A skiff landed at the boat-shed at about two this morning. Your reed tell was trampled. A lean man in a brown coat, and four others. At the four o'clock low, two went out along the causeway and worked under the road at the culvert for an hour. I saw them cut the timber edging at the posts and tie lines to them, lines that run back to the shed." She draws a line in the air. "My guess is the edging drops when a wagon is on the culvert. Wagon and horses go into the channel, with the tide coming back. At dawn three took the skiff off toward the creek mouth, and two stayed in the shed. No tall man in a grey cloak. Not yet."

The causeway opens around two. It is just past noon, and your guards can reach the landward reeds before then. You have three slots, three Inspirations, and Kit. The trap is set for you, and you know where it is. What does Wren do?

sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. input.add_to_description: Day 15 ~11 AM, Marl Sedge's report from the far-bank boat-shed: the reed tell was swept aside by a skiff keel at about 3 AM. She counted five men in the shed by dawn: Sparrow (brown coat), three pikemen, and a fifth, tall and hooded in grey, who arrived by a second boat at first light and has not left. They have a hand-winch and two coils of rope in the shed, as if to chain the culvert, and a black-hulled rowboat (not the cutter). At about 9 AM she saw the Heron's Tithe's grey sail standing off beyond the creek mouth in the main channel, waiting for high water at ~10:40. The Grey Cloak is therefore likely present himself, and the cutter can come up the channel at flood to cut off retreat across the water.

entries.text: notebook: updated Gannet Causeway

Corvin says nothing on the road. When you ride up and murmur your warning, he lifts two fingers to his brow, almost a salute. Pell, on the other side of the wagon, says to the sky that he would be glad to gag anyone who asks. The guards laugh under their breath at your road song, and by the fourth verse two of them are humming it flat. The column goes on through the marsh country in a thin, bright morning.

At eleven the land drops away to the flats, and the Gannet Causeway lies ahead, a dark thread across silver mud and standing water, still half under the tide. The six guards peel off into the landward reeds with their crossbows, as arranged. You leave the wagon behind them and go to find Marl.

She is where she said, flat in a ditch among the reeds with mud to her eyes. She speaks very low, without turning her head.

"Your tell's gone. A skiff keel swept the reeds aside about three. By dawn there were five in the shed. The brown-coat. Three with pikes. And a tall one in grey, hood up, who came in by a second boat at first light and hasn't stirred." She counts it on her fingers. "They've a hand-winch and two coils of rope in there. Looks to me like they mean to chain the culvert shut behind you." A pause. "And at nine, I saw a grey sail standing off beyond the creek mouth, waiting for the flood. High water is twenty to eleven. That's her coming up the channel now, or it will be within the hour."

So the trap is as you were told, and more than you were told. The Grey Cloak is on the far bank himself. The cutter can come up the tidal channel to cut off the water behind you, and the winch can seal the culvert ahead.

It is nearly eleven. The causeway opens around two. You've three slots, three Inspirations, Kit, Pell, six guards in the reeds, and a wagon that must cross in the open. What does Wren do?

At about 11 AM a grey sail stood off beyond the creek mouth, then dropped below the horizon. So the Grey Cloak knows the place and the hour; his men may be waiting on the far bank now. Marl crossed back by wading the ebb channel at ~12:45.

entries.text: notebook: updated Gannet Causeway

You ride up beside the wagon and murmur your warning. Corvin doesn't look round. "Child," he says, mildly, "I haven't said a word that wasn't in a plan since I was twenty." Pell, riding on the other side, makes a small noise that might be a cough. You give the order to move out, hum the road song low, and Kit's flat, true voice joins you for a verse. Behind you two of the guards pick up the tune without meaning to.

The road is dull. It runs through marsh and drained fields under a high white sky, and by the time you pass the last farm, the air smells of salt mud. You send the six guards ahead in twos, as the arbiter agreed, to take the landward reeds before you show yourselves. A little before one the column halts at the causeway's mouth, the wagon drawn off the road behind a hedge of tamarisk. The flats ahead are shining, the channel is still brimming, and the road runs out across them like a pale thread.

Marl finds you before you find her. She comes wading up the channel's edge in wet grey, mud to her thighs, having crossed on the ebb, and she gives her report squatting by your stirrup in her flat voice. About two in the night a skiff with three men landed at the boat-shed. At the four o'clock low, one of them, a lean man in a brown coat, walked the causeway with a knotted cord and measured the culvert, plainly, as a man measures a gate. At dawn they left, trampling through the reeds you laid across the stake's path. And at about eleven this morning a grey sail stood off beyond the creek mouth, a long way out, and then dropped below the horizon.

"He knows the place and the hour," she says. "He may be across there now."

It is ten to one. The causeway will open at about two. The six guards are in the landward reeds, Pell is with the wagon, and Corvin is sitting very still on the bench. You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots, three Inspirations, Kit beside you, and the lure in your saddlebag. What does Wren do?

The barn is burning. You run along its shadow to the north side and set your back against the wall, so nothing can come up behind you. Then you point at the black stretch of hedge where the burning rag came from and speak the Lantern-Bearer's word. Violet light blooms across the hedge-bank. Pell's guards don't wait to be told twice. Two spears thud into Sparrow and he grunts, bloodied, at a third of his strength gone. Two more spears take the lit pikeman, who turns and bolts for the river with only a few hit points left. It's round 2 and your turn. You hold Faerie Fire by concentration, with two slots, three Bardic Inspirations, a rapier, a dagger and the lamp-staff. Sparrow is lit and bloodied about thirty feet away, with two pikemen at your sides. The prisoners are out of the barn. Kit is with them, and Pell's guards are firing from the yard. It's eleven-thirty at night on Day 16. What does Wren do?

entries.text: notebook: updated Brother Osric

You climb down, press a coin on the drover, and take Kit and Pell into the lee of the stable. Pell listens with his arms folded. "Splitting the column is a risk," he says, "but a wounded man on a stolen hack and a priest with a long memory is a worse one." He nods. "Take Dunn and Harl, they've the best horses. I'll keep four on the wagon, Tam in irons, and the prisoners on the bench between my two best spears. We'll be on the road an hour behind you by noon, and at the manor by the evening bell." Then, dry as ever: "If you leave me a song, I'll make do."

You write the note on a leaf of the blank paper and seal it with a thumb of wax: "Sparrow comes to Osric. Bar the chapel, keep him inside the manor. W." The landlord's boy, the best rider in the yard, takes it at a gallop with a lantern on his saddle-bow. You pay him two silver for it, and he's gone before the coins stop ringing. You see to Ember's feed yourself, count your slots by habit, and take a bed under the eaves.

You're up at half past five and away in the grey. You, Kit, Dunn and Harl ride hard along the river road. The horses breathe smoke in the cold, and the stubble fields, mills and wet hedges go by in blurs. Twice you change pace to rest the animals. Nothing lies in wait, no brown coat and no grey sail, and your Perception finds only rooks.

At noon on Day 18 you top a low rise and Thornhallow lies below, grey and walled on its bend of the Marrow, with the green chapel roof inside the wall and smoke from the village chimneys. The gatehouse pennant, green and white, hangs limp. The gate itself is shut, and that's wrong for midday. There are men on the wall-walk with bows, and at the gate a boy in a page's livery runs out of the wicket, stops, and points straight at you.

You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots and three Inspirations. Your note got here first. What does Wren do?

input.add_to_description: Day 17-18: Wren's night note ('Sparrow comes to Osric, bar the chapel and keep him inside the manor') reached the gatehouse about four in the morning by a Vantry rider. Lord Edric moved Osric into the manor and posted men at the chapel. Just before dawn on Day 18 a lean man in a brown coat was seen trying the chapel's vestry window, was challenged, and fled on a horse toward the river. Wren, Kit and two guards reached the gate about 1 PM on Day 18, ahead of Pell's wagon.

entries.text: notebook: updated Thornhallow

You climb down off the table, press a coin into the drover's hand, and take Kit and Pell aside by the stable door. Pell hears you out and rubs his jaw. He doesn't like splitting the escort. But the wagon can't outrun a horse, and he knows it. "Two of my best, then," he says. "Hurl and Wick. They're light and they won't tire. I'll bring the wagon and keep both prisoners in chains. Ansel stays on the bench where I can see his hands." Then, dryly: "Don't get killed before the assize. The arbiter would be cross."

You write your note on the back of a tavern bill in your small, careful hand: "Sparrow comes to Osric. Bar the chapel and keep him inside the manor. W." You fold it, seal it with a drop of the landlord's wax and your thumb, and a Vantry rider is in the saddle on the best horse in the yard before the candle has burned a finger down. You check your slots and Ember's feed, and take a bed in the loft with Kit across the trapdoor.

You're up at half past five. The four of you ride hard, with Kit and the two guards on rested horses and Ember galloping as if she'd waited all her life for it. You stop twice to water the horses and walk them. The river road runs flat and straight through harvested fields and over two wooden bridges, and you see no brown coat and no grey sail. At one in the afternoon on Day 18, the green and white pennant of Thornhallow shows over the trees.

The gatehouse is awake and alert. Two men in Verrel livery stand at the gate with spears, and a third watches from the wall. When they see the riders they don't lower the portcullis, and one of them runs for the manor. Behind the gate the village is quiet, with shutters half drawn and no children in the lane. Lord Edric comes out onto the manor steps with a clerk behind him, thinner than you remember and in a plain dark coat. Your night rider is in the yard with a bandaged hand.

You go down to the yard and find Pell grey with the road, leaning on the wagon. "Ansel goes up to the study first, with two guards. Corvin waits in the gatehouse under watch until I send for him," you tell him quietly. He grunts. "Both ends of a rope, then." He sends Corvin off with two men, and Corvin goes without comment, looking at the manor's lit windows the way a man looks at a stage he has sold tickets to.

You walk Ansel up to Lord Edric's door yourself. He is straight-backed and his chains clink softly on the stair. "He's ready to tell it his own way, my lord," you say at the threshold. "Ansel, say it plain, and let Osric hear every word." Then you take your place just inside, back to the wall, a hand on the lamp-staff, with Kit beside you.

Lord Edric stands behind his desk, with Osric at his elbow and the register open on the blotter. A lamp burns. Nobody sits. Ansel stands in the middle of the floor, and the two men have the same chin, though neither seems to have noticed.

"I am Ansel Verrel," he says. "Hugh Verrel's son, by Joan Reeve, a ferryman's daughter, lawfully wed in your chapel." His voice stays quiet and steady. "My father took a boat the night before the wedding feast and was never seen again. Your father scraped my name from that book and paid my mother to be silent. She took the coin. She was poor, and she had a boy." He looks at Osric. "I did not come to take your house, cousin. I came to have my name put back where it was written, and I did it in the worst way a man could."

Edric says nothing for a long time. Osric lays his finger on the scraped line and nods once, slowly, to himself.

"I thought the proof was in the chapel's founding lamp," Ansel says. "The old chaplain hid Hugh's marriage lines there, my mother told me. Elowen Ashgrove took the lamp to the sea and found them. She wouldn't give them to me." His mouth twists. "She said I wanted them as a sword, not as the truth. She was right, and I struck her for it."

The lamp hisses. Edric lowers himself into his chair as though his knees have been cut. "A ferryman's daughter," he says, to no one. "A chaplain's lamp." He looks at you, and his eyes are wet and angry and terribly tired. "Mistress Wren. You said this man would tell it himself, and he has. What do you say I should do with him?"

It's twenty-five to seven on Day 18. You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots and three Inspirations. Corvin waits in the gatehouse, Sparrow sleeps in the cellar, Hale is locked below, and Dame Crowe's assize is twelve days off. What does Wren do?

input.add_to_description: Day 18 dusk, Thornhallow study (Edric, Osric, Wren, Kit present): Ansel told it himself. He is the son of Hugh Verrel (Aldous's eldest) and Joan, a ferryman's daughter whom Hugh married secretly. Hugh died in a river accident before Ansel was born; Edric's father Rolf had the baptism scraped to protect the Aldermere claim, paid Joan to leave, and told the house Hugh died unmarried. Ansel grew up on the lower Marrow, made money as a trader, became Elowen's patron. He took the name 'Aldous the younger' because it was a dead child's name that no one would look for. Osric confirmed the founding lamp of the chapel was given by Aldous to the Lantern-Bearer's road-priests about forty years ago. Edric said he will have a true entry written for Ansel; Ansel still faces Crowe for the attacks and Garrow's death.

In the yard you meet Pell by the wagon, in the red light of the setting sun. He listens and nods. "Ansel up to the study with two spears, Corvin in the gatehouse. That's cleaner than I'd have done it." Corvin watches from the bench with a dry little smile, as if he'd expected to be put second. He says nothing as two guards walk him to the gatehouse.

You walk Ansel to Lord Edric's door yourself, with Kit a step behind. His chains clink on the stair. At the threshold you say, "He's ready to tell it his own way, my lord. Ansel, say it plain, and let Osric hear every word." Then you stand just inside with your back to the wall, your hand on the lamp-staff and Kit beside you.

Edric is on his feet behind the desk with Osric at his elbow. For a moment neither Verrel speaks. They have the same long chin and the same crease between the brows, thirty years apart. Then Ansel says it, without ornament.

"My father was Hugh, your father's elder brother. He married Joan Marl, a ferryman's daughter, at a river chapel with two witnesses, and drowned before I was born. Your father had my baptism scraped and paid my mother to leave the county, because the house was building an Aldermere ancestor and could not afford an eldest son who was a ferryman's grandchild." time: 1 hour later: Day 18, 6:45:06 PM

Corvin goes off between two spears, looking at the lit windows as though he were already selling the scene. You walk Ansel up the stair yourself and stop at Lord Edric's door. "He's ready to tell it his own way, my lord. Ansel, say it plain, and let Osric hear every word."

You take your place just inside the door with your back to the wall, your hand on the lamp-staff and Kit beside you. The candles are lit. Edric sits stiff as a post behind the desk, with Osric at his elbow and the register open between them.

Ansel does not sit. The chain makes a small noise as he stands in front of the desk. He looks at Edric for a long moment, then speaks without any of the smoothness he used on the causeway.

"I am Ansel, son of Hugh Verrel and of Joan Harker, a ferryman's daughter. They married privately, the year before your father found them out. Hugh drowned at twenty-four, not nineteen. Your father struck the marriage from the paper and the child with it, so the Aldermere claim would look clean. To explain the hole, he invented a cousin, 'Aldous the younger', lost abroad, and took the name from a servant's child who was already in the churchyard." His thumb turns the ring. "My mother told me when she was dying, and she gave me this, which was Hugh's. I was sixteen. I have spent thirty-four years wanting what was mine, and some of those years I made a fool's work of it."

He tells the rest more quickly. He met Elowen as her patron, and she was the only person who ever laughed at his sums. He gave her what proof he had of his birth, and she kept it safe. Later he took the dead child's name because a man called Aldous the younger could walk into Thornhallow and be believed, if the one leaf that proved the child dead could be burned. Hale was his go-between and Sparrow his knife. He hired the swords. "I never ordered the girl's death," he says, "though I wasn't careful enough about who did. I won't ask you to believe me."

Edric has not moved. When he speaks, his voice is hoarse. "I confessed to the assessor that my house was built on a lie. I did not know it was built on a grave as well." He looks at the register and at the scraped line, then at the ring, and at last at his cousin's face, and you watch him see the chin. "I will not strike this line again," he says. "Whatever Dame Crowe decides about the rest. Sit down, Ansel. For God's sake, sit."

Ansel sits, and for the first time since the causeway his shoulders come down. Osric has begun to write.

input.add_to_description: Day 20: the Fenwick Ferry ferryman says a lean grey-coated man with a notched ear and two heavy men crossed to the north bank at dawn with a satchel and a hand-cart's load, in a hired skiff, heading upriver toward the Ashby road. The cart was left empty at the ferry landing. Crake has Oake's real papers.

entries.text: notebook: updated Dunstan Crake
time: 8 hours 10 minutes later: Day 20, 5:30:06 PM

You ask Lyle to hold the chest closed until you're back, then borrow two fast horses from the bridge-house stable and take Kit and a young watchman named Dobb. "If the clerk comes at noon," you tell Lyle, "he opens it in front of you and the notary, and I'll be back by dusk." Lyle nods, and her keys chime.

The east road is a stony, sunny drove road, and it has seen a lot of carts. Your Survival is a 5, and the rut you thought you were following goes cold in the first mile. A hand-cart wheel looks like a dozen other wheels on a road like this. At the east gate your Persuasion is an 8, and the gate-keeper, a sour man with a swollen jaw, tells you six carts pass each hour and he doesn't mark them. He remembers nothing about a grey coat, and he is not interested in remembering.

You ride on regardless. At each tollhouse you ask the same question and get a shrug, until the third, where an old woman peeling turnips remembers a lean man with a ruined ear going by at dusk toward Fenwick Ferry, "in a hurry, with a cart and no manners." It's three hours of dust. At Fenwick the ferryman, a bandy-legged man with a pipe, says that a lean man with a notched ear and two heavy men crossed at dawn to the north bank in a hired skiff, with a satchel and as many boxes as the skiff would hold. "Upriver," he says, "toward the Ashby road." The hand-cart still sits empty at his landing, with its wheel-rims scraped bright. He doesn't know where they went after the far bank.

You ride back in the afternoon heat. On the road, four miles from Marrowford, a thin man in a clerk's coat comes stumbling toward you with his hands raised. He is about forty, ink-stained, and he is weeping. Corbin Sedley. "Please," he says. "Please, I'll tell you everything. They left me at the ferry. He said I'd be a loose end." He wipes his face. "I'd sooner hang than be left twice."

You take him up behind Dobb and bring him to the bridge-house by half past five. Lyle receives him with her keys quiet in her hand. Crowe's clerk has been and gone: the notary says he opened the chest at noon before the Warden and himself, and it held grain ledgers and nothing else. You expected that.

It's half past five on Day 20. You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots and three Inspirations. Sedley is under Lyle's seal and has not yet said a word of it. Pell's wagon with Corvin is due at the gates, and Crake and the real papers are somewhere on the north bank. What does Wren do?

input.description: Disused fulling-mill on Hawk Lane, about six miles east of Marrowford, with a stone landing on a navigable tributary that joins the Marrow. Day 20: Dunstan Crake, clerk Corbin Sedley and a hand-cart with Oake's real papers are heading here; the gate-boy's found scrap, a clerk's cart list, says the papers go downriver by barge from the landing to the Heron's Tithe at Sedge Creek by the 24th.

entries.text: notebook: created an entry for Cressy Mill; added 2 relationships to Cressy Mill
sheet: gained 1 × Crumpled carter's list from the east gate (7 boxes 'A.', 2 tin cases, 1 map; 'Hawk Lane, Cressy Mill landing, barge by the 22nd, Heron by the 24th')
time: 1 hour 40 minutes later: Day 20, 11:00:06 AM

You ask Lyle to hold the chest unopened until the clerk comes, and to open it in front of her and a notary. "I'll be back by dusk," you say. You borrow two fast horses from the bridge-house stable, and Kit and a lanky watchman named Orrin ride out with you.

On the east road you try to read the cart rut, and your Survival is a 10. Half the carts in the county have crossed this road since yesterday, and the rut tells you nothing. But your Persuasion with the gatekeepers is a natural 20, and the east gate's keeper, a stout, garrulous man, takes to you at once. He remembers a hand-cart with a tarpaulin at dusk yesterday, pulled by two men, with a lean grey-coated man walking ahead, a notch in his left ear, and a thin ink-stained clerk riding the tail. "Clerk fussed the whole way," he says. "Kept shifting the lashings." His boy, a snub-nosed lad of ten, tugs your sleeve and holds up a crumpled sheet he picked up from the gutter. "He dropped it, mistress. It's a list."

It is a carter's list in a looped clerk's hand. It reads: seven boxes marked "A.", two tin cases, one map. And below it: "Hawk Lane. Cressy Mill landing. Barge by the 22nd. Heron by the 24th." The loops are the same ones on the old letter and the tally-sheet. Sedley's hand again. They aren't hiding Oake's real books. They are sending them by water to the Heron's Tithe.

You ride east along Hawk Lane for six miles of wheat stubble and alder hedges. At eleven, from a rise, you see Cressy Mill below. It is a grey stone fulling-mill with a broken wheel, a barn, a walled yard, and a stone landing on a small river where a flat-bottomed barge lies moored with its mast stepped. A thread of smoke comes up the mill chimney. The hand-cart stands in the yard with its tarpaulin thrown back, and two heavy-shouldered men lounge by the barn door with their coats off. There is no sign of Crake or the clerk. Kit leans from the saddle and says low, "Two men outside. At least two more in."

It's eleven in the morning on Day 20. You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots and three Inspirations, and Orrin the watchman is beside you with a pike. Pell's wagon is still on the road behind. What does Wren do?

She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Fey Ancestry: You have advantage on saving throws against being charmed, and magic cannot put you to sleep.
Skill Versatility: You gain proficiency in two skills of your choice.

Bardic Inspiration (d6): You can inspire others through stirring words or music. To do so, you use a bonus action on your turn to choose one creature other than yourself within 60 feet of you who can hear you. That creature gains one Bardic Inspiration die, a d6. Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. The creature can wait until after it rolls the d20 before deciding to use the Bardic Inspiration die, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails. Once the Bardic Inspiration die is rolled, it is lost. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Charisma modifier (a minimum of once). You regain any expended uses when you finish a long rest.  Your Bardic Inspiration die changes when you reach certain levels in this class. The die becomes a d8 at 5th level, a d10 at 10th level, and a d12 at 15th level. At level 2: Bardic Inspiration die d6.
Jack of All Trades: Starting at 2nd level, you can add half your proficiency bonus, rounded down, to any ability check you make that doesn't already include your proficiency bonus.

Song of Rest (d6): Beginning at 2nd level, you can use soothing music or oration to help revitalize your wounded allies during a short rest. If you or any friendly creatures who can hear your performance regain hit points at the end of the short rest by spending one or more Hit Dice, each of those creatures regains an extra 1d6 hit points.  The extra hit points increase when you reach certain levels in this class: to 1d8 at 9th level, to 1d10 at 13th level, and to 1d12 at 17th level. At level 2: extra 1d6 hit points.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

line:
I ask Lyle to hold the chest unopened until I'm back and decide to follow the hand-cart rut myself with Kit and a watchman, because a loaded cart is slow and I want to catch whoever holds Oake's real books before they disappear. I borrow two fast horses from the bridge-house stable and tell Lyle, "If the clerk arrives at noon, he opens the chest in front of you and a notary, and I'll be back by dusk."

On the road I read the rut for depth and freshness, and ask each gate-keeper along the east road if a grey-coated man with a notched ear passed with a clerk and a hand-cart.

input.add_to_description: Day 20: Wren (Survival 12) tracked the cart rut from Oake's alley out the east gate to Fenmoor Ferry, two hours' ride. The ferryman (reluctant; Persuasion 10 failed) admitted only that a grey-coated man with a notched ear, a thin ink-stained clerk and a covered hand-cart crossed the Fenmoor landing at dusk on Day 19 and were taken downriver in a hired skiff after dark; the cart was left empty in a ditch. Wren infers they are racing downriver toward Sedge Creek and the Heron's Tithe, which is held until the 24th.

time: 4 hours later: Day 20, 1:20:06 PM

You ask Lyle to hold the chest unopened until you're back. She grunts that it opens at noon in front of her and a notary, with or without you, and you agree. You borrow two fast horses from the bridge-house stable and take Kit and a young watchman named Brek with you. Out through the east gate you go, with the sun climbing.

The gatekeeper remembers the cart at once. A thin clerk and a lean grey-coated man with a notch in his ear took a loaded hand-cart through at dusk yesterday, just before the gate closed. "Paid the toll in good silver," he says, "and the clerk never stopped looking over his shoulder."

On the road, you read the rut. Your Survival is a 12, just enough. The wheels sank deep in the soft verge, so the cart was heavy, and they kept it away from the main track as if they didn't want company. It leads east through water-meadows for two hours to Fenmoor Ferry, a squat landing with a rope and a flat boat.

The cart sits abandoned in a ditch below the landing with its tailboard open and nothing in it. The ferryman, a squint-eyed man called Orrin, is mending a net. When you ask your questions he spits. Your Persuasion is a 10, and a coin and Brek's badge are not enough to open him all the way. "Took a boat last night," he says at last. "Hired my cousin's skiff, after dark. Downriver. That's all I know and all I saw." He won't say whether they stopped at the bend, or who met them. But a man who has a clerk, a cart of papers and a hired boat, heading downriver with four days of current in front of him, has somewhere to be by the 24th.

It's twenty past one on Day 20. You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots and three Inspirations, and 77 gp, 8 sp and 2 cp. The chest was due to be opened at noon. Crake, the clerk and the books are somewhere on the river, bound, you think, for Sedge Creek and Cobb Harrow's cutter. What does Wren do?
